newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says won't protect islands protest flotilla.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says won't protect islands protest flotilla.

text.p: The Taiwan government on Saturday rejected a request by protest activists for protection when they sail to challenge Japan's claim to a disputed East China Sea island group, but said the marine police will stand by to help.

"(The marine police will) stand by at the most suitable location that they can function. In case any emergency or ship accident occurs, we will save them," vice interior minister Yang Pao-fa said on state television.

The state-run Central News Agency on Saturday reported that the marine police headquarters rejected activists' request to to protect them when they sail on Sunday to reach the islands claimed by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus and by Japan as the Senkakus.
The agency quoted the police headquarters as saying the protest voyage was illegal and against the government's policy.
The police headquarters had tried to persuade the activists to stop their planned voyage for safety reasons due to high winds in the Diaoyus area, the agency said.
Sunday's sailing and a planned Monday landing attempt were not eligible for marine protection, officials had said.

They said fishing boats were not allowed to ferry non-fishermen and pleasure boats were not given marine protection beyond 24 nautical miles off Taiwan's shores -- putting the disputed islands far beyond reach.
The islands lie 200 km (125 miles) northeast of Taiwan.
Japanese patrols have repulsed private boats trying to land Hong Kong and Taiwan activists on the islands.
Pressure on Japan to defuse tensions escalated with the September 26 death of Hong Kong activist David Chan, who drowned after jumping off a protest ship that had been prevented from landing.
In Tokyo, the Japanese government on Friday sought to ease tensions with China and Taiwan by saying it would not recognise an offending lighthouse as part of its maritime safety system.
But Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said the concession did not alter Tokyo's claim of sovereignty to the islands.
Separately, Taiwan negotiators said they had failed to reach agreement with their Japanese counterparts in talks over fishing rights and other issues stemming from the sovereignty row.
The cluster of uninhabited rocky outcrops in the East China Sea has kindled fiery passions among Chinese communities since Japanese rightwingers built a lighthouse and planted flags there in July.
